composed.prompt_en: Create an original illustrated character-design board for a small nonhuman landslide-warning companion and an adult geologist. The first glance is a broad field-action panel where the low six-legged creature braces across a scree slope while three flexible wind vanes flare upslope. The second look reveals graphite tips on those vanes drawing a wind rose into the geologist's dusted survey card as the body pivots. The three back vanes bend progressively toward the incoming gust, their graphite tips mark source direction, and the creature turns its wedge head toward the occluded ravine. The wide vanes improve wind sensing but catch on a narrow rock cleft, so the creature folds them and loses that warning range while crawling through. Rows of mica flakes sorted by size beside its resting hollow and shallow six-foot tracks across loose shale record how it gathers ballast. Show the small six-legged companion presses one foreclaw onto the inclinometer plate toward the adult geologist's slope-measuring tool; the tool needle jumps as the geologist plants a warning pennant above the unstable scree. Six low splayed feet with hooked inner toes side-step across scree while stone-filled ankle pouches keep the body from rolling downslope. This is a functional field-companion design board with an adult geologist. The sensory vanes also become the creature's physical plotting tool instead of a decorative crest. Each vane tip scores a separate direction line into the survey card, and the creature must pivot its whole weighted body to complete the diagram. Make the flared three-vane silhouette and braced six-foot stance dominant, then let the survey-tool contact and sorted mica emerge as secondary evidence. Keep the board background quiet and omit personality labels, species lore, costume decoration, and unrelated accessories. Draw hard structural edges on hooked feet, vane hinges, and tool contact; use flexible tapering strokes only along vane membranes and wind marks. Repeat one graphite-vane material rule: clean tips before sensing, dark contact lines while plotting, and worn leeward tips after repeated use. Representation one is a large three-quarter field-action view of the creature warning the adult geologist beside the inclinometer. Representation two is a four-view front, side, top, and folded-crawl comparison with small functional callouts but no readable labels. Across every view, preserve three crescent vanes, a wedge head with no human face, six splayed hooked feet, and two stone-filled ankle pouches. In the smallest callout, reduce each vane to one bold crescent and each foot to one hooked block while preserving vane direction and six-point stance. Show open vanes facing an upslope gust in the action view and folded vanes with a lower crawl in the narrow-cleft view. The board's repeatable signature is this: three living vanes draw the warning before either partner points.
